Remark 11

One must take care not to confuse a fundamental pro-object \(P\) (which is not endowed with a group structure, and is connected) with the fundamental pro-group (which is a pro-group, and in general not connected). More precisely, \(G\) is connected if and only if \(\pi_F\) acting on itself by inner automorphisms is transitive, i.e. if \(\pi\) is reduced to the identity element, or again if \(\mathscr{C}\) is equivalent to the category of finite sets. Another essential difference is that \(G\) is determined up to unique isomorphism, while \(P\) is only determined up to non-unique isomorphism.

Let \(E\) be a finite set and consider the constant functor on the groupoid \(\Gamma\), with value \(E\): by virtue of 8 it defines an object of \(\mathscr{C}\), denoted \(E_{\mathscr{C}}\), and which may also be interpreted as the sum of \(E\) copies of the final object \(e_{\mathscr{C}}\) of \(\mathscr{C}\). One may regard \(E_{\mathscr{C}}\) as a functor in \(E\), from the category of finite sets to the category \(\mathscr{C}\), and this functor is exact, hence transforms finite groups into \(\mathscr{C}\)-groups, etc. If therefore \(X\) is an object of \(\mathscr{C}\) on which the finite group \(G\) acts on the right, one sees that one may regard \(X\) as an object of \(\mathscr{C}\) having a \(\mathscr{C}\)-group of operators on the right \(G_{\mathscr{C}}\). One will therefore say, by extension of a general terminology relative to objects with \(\mathscr{C}\)-groups of operators, that \(X\) is formally principal homogeneous under \(G\) if and only if \(X\) is formally principal homogeneous under \(G_{\mathscr{C}}\), i.e. if the canonical morphism

\[ X\times G_{\mathscr{C}} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\times X \]

deduced from the operation of \(G_{\mathscr{C}}\) on \(X\) on the right, is an isomorphism. One says that \(X\) is principal homogeneous under \(G\) if it is so under \(G_{\mathscr{C}}\), i.e. if it is so formally, and if moreover the quotient \(X/G=X/G_{\mathscr{C}}\) is \(e_{\mathscr{C}}\). If one fixes a fundamental functor, whence an equivalence of \(\mathscr{C}\) with a category \(\mathscr{C}(\pi)\), \(X\) corresponds to a set on which \(\pi\) acts on the left continuously, say \(E=F(X)\). To make \(G\) act on \(X\) on the right then amounts to making \(G\) act on the set \(E\) on the right, in such a way that the operations of \(G\) commute with those of \(\pi\). One then observes at once that \(X\) is principal homogeneous under \(G\) if and only if the set \(E\) is a principal homogeneous space under \(G\), i.e. if and only if \(G\) acts on it in a simply transitive way. In the typical case \(\mathscr{C}=\mathscr{C}(\pi)\), this means that \(X\) is isomorphic to a quotient of \(\pi\) by an invariant subgroup.

Remark

Of course, it is most often preferable to reason directly on fibred categories without using explicit cleavages, which in particular dispenses with appealing, for the simple notion of \(\mathscr{E}\)-functor or of cartesian \(\mathscr{E}\)-functor, to a cumbersome interpretation as above. It is in order to avoid unbearable heaviness, and in order to obtain more intrinsic statements, that we have had to give up starting, as in [2], from the notion of cloven category (called “fibred category” in loc. cit. ), which passes into second place in favour of that of fibred category. It is moreover probable that, contrary to the usage still predominant now, tied to old habits of thought, it will end up proving more convenient, in universal problems, not to place the emphasis on one solution supposed to be chosen once and for all, but to place all solutions on an equal footing.

Remarks 4

Of course, the results of this section are well known. On the other hand, J-P. Serre has shown [10] that when \(X\) is a smooth projective unirational variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, \(X\) is simply connected. His proof is transcendental in that it uses the Hodge symmetry theorem.

[Added in 2003 (MR) Let us restrict ourselves to the case of an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic \(p\geqslant 0\). In characteristic \(p>0\), the definition of \(k\)-unirational variety given above is that of \(k\)-variety weakly unirational, as opposed to that of \(k\)-variety strongly unirational, where one moreover assumes that \(K'\) is a separable extension of \(K\).

In the case of dimension \(2\), there exist projective and smooth surfaces, weakly unirational, which have a non-trivial fundamental group (finite by 1.3) and which are therefore not rational (T. Shioda, On unirationality of supersingular surfaces, Math. Ann. 225 (1977), p. 155–159.). On the other hand a strongly unirational surface is rational: this follows from Castelnuovo's rationality criterion, extended to characteristic \(p>0\) by O. Zariski (cf. J-P. Serre, Sém. Bourbaki nº 146, 1957 and Œuvres–Collected papers, vol. 1, p. 467).

Over the field \(\mathbf{C}\) of complex numbers, one knows examples of projective and smooth varieties of dimension \(\geqslant 3\) which are unirational and non- rational (cf. P. Deligne, Variétés unirationnelles non rationnelles [d'après M. Artin et D. Mumford], Sém. Bourbaki nº 402, 1971-72, Lecture Notes vol. 317). This is the case in particular of a smooth cubic hypersurface in the projective space \(\mathbf{P}^4\). Some of these examples extend to characteristic \(>0\) to give strongly unirational non-rational varieties (cf. J.P. Murre, Reduction of the proof of the non-rationality of a non singular cubic threefold to a result of Mumford, Compositio Math. 27 (1973), p. 63–82).

Let \(V\) be a normal, integral projective \(k\)-variety. One says that \(V\) is rationally connected, if there exist an integral \(k\)-scheme of finite type \(T\) and a \(k\)-morphism \(F : T\times\mathbf{P}^1\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) such that the morphism:

\[ \tag*{(1)} \begin{split} T \times\mathbf{P}^1\times\mathbf{P}^1&\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\times V\\ (t, u, u')&\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}(F(t,u), F(t,u')) \end{split} \]

is dominant. In particular, through two sufficiently general rational points of \(V\) passes a rational curve. The terminology is justified by the fact that if \(V\) is rationally connected, one can join two rational points by a finite chain of rational curves. If \(k\) is of characteristic \(p>0\), one strengthens the preceding definition by requiring that the map (1) be generically smooth. One then obtains the notion of separably rationally connected variety. Kollár has shown that separably rationally connected varieties have a trivial algebraic fundamental group (cf. O. Debarre, Variétés rationnellement connexes [d'après T. Graber, J. Harris, J. Starr et A.J. de Jong], Sém. Bourbaki nº 906, 2001-2002).]

If \(\overline{s}\) is a geometric point of \(S\), \(y\) a maximal point of \(Y_{\overline{s}}\), one denotes by \(\overline{S}\) the strict localization of \(S\) at \(\overline{s}\), \(\overline{X}\) the strict localization of \(X\) at \(\overline{y}\), \(\overline{U}=U\times_X \overline{X}\), \(\overline{V}=V\times_X\overline{X}\). If the condition of 1.1 is satisfied at the geometric points above the maximal points of \(S\), it follows from 5 below that \(\overline{V}\) is a covering of \(\overline{U}\) tamely ramified over \(\overline{X}\) relatively to \(\overline{S}\); consequently \(V\) is an étale covering of \(U\) tamely ramified over \(X\) relatively to \(S\).

If \(\overline{s}\) is a geometric point of \(S\), \(y\) a maximal point of \(Y_{\overline{s}}\), one denotes by \(K\) the field of fractions of \(\mathscr{O}_{X_{\overline{s}},y}\). One will sometimes say, by abuse of language, that \(F\) is prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\). proposals.before: Exposés I to IV present the local notions of étale morphism and smooth morphism; they hardly use the language of schemes, set forth in Chapter I of the Éléments2. Exposé V presents the axiomatic description of the fundamental group of a scheme, useful even in the classical case where this scheme reduces to the spectrum of a field, where one finds a most convenient reformulation of the usual Galois theory. Exposés VI and VIII present descent theory, which has taken on a growing importance in Algebraic Geometry in these last years, and which could render analogous services in Analytic Geometry and in Topology. It is fitting to point out that Exposé VII had not been written, and its substance is incorporated in a work of J. Giraud (Méthode de la Descente, Bull. Soc. Math. France, Mémoire 2, 1964, viii + 150 p.). In Exposé IX, one studies more specifically the descent of étale morphisms, obtaining a systematic approach for theorems of the Van Kampen type for the fundamental group, which appear here as mere translations of descent theorems. It is essentially a matter of a procedure for computing the fundamental group of a connected scheme \(X\), equipped with a surjective and proper morphism, say \(X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), in terms of the fundamental groups of the connected components of \(X'\) and of the fibre products \(X'\times_X X'\), \(X'\times_X X'\times_X X'\), and of the homomorphisms induced between these groups by the canonical simplicial morphisms between the preceding schemes. Exposé X gives the theory of the specialization of the fundamental group, for a proper and smooth morphism, whose most striking result consists in the determination (up to little) of the fundamental group of a smooth algebraic curve in characteristic \(p>0\), thanks to the result known by transcendental means in characteristic zero. Exposé XI gives some examples and complements, notably making explicit in cohomological form the theory of the coverings of Kummer, and that of Artin-Schreier. For other comments on the text, see the Avertissement to the multigraphed version, which follows the present Introduction.

Remarques 18

Rappelons (I 1) que si \(X\) est un préschéma au-dessus de \(S\), on introduit les faisceaux quasi-cohérents d'algèbres \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^n=\mathscr{O}_{X\times_S X}/\mathscr{I}_X^{n+1}\) sur \(X\), (où \(\mathscr{I}_X\) désigne le faisceau d'idéaux qui définit la diagonale dans \(X\times_S X\)), considéré comme faisceau de \(\mathscr{O}_X\)-algèbres grâce à la première projection \(\mathrm{pr}_1\colon X\times_S X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\). Les \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^n\) forment un système projectif d'Algèbres sur \(X\), dont la limite projective est notée \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^{\infty}\) et n'est autre que le faisceau structural du complété formel de \(X\times_S X\) le long de la diagonale (en supposant maintenant \(X\) localement de type fini sur \(S\), donc les \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^n\) cohérents). Dire que \(X\) est différentiablement lisse sur \(S\) (i.e. que le morphisme diagonal \(\Delta_{X/S}\) est une immersion régulière) signifie aussi que \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^{\infty}\) est régulier, en tant que faisceau d'algèbres augmenté vers \(\mathscr{O}_X\), i.e. que \(\mathit{\Omega}_{X/S}^1\) est localement libre et l'homomorphisme surjectif canonique

\[ S_{\mathscr{O}_X}(\mathit{\Omega}_{X/S}^1)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathrm{gr}_*(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^{\infty}) \]

est un isomorphisme, ou enfin que tout point de \(X\) a un voisinage ouvert sur lequel le faisceau d'algèbres augmentées \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^{\infty}\) soit isomorphe à un faisceau \(\mathscr{O}_X[[t_1,\dots,t_n]]\).

Soit \(s\) une section de \(X\) sur \(S\), \(\mathscr{J}\) le faisceau d'idéaux sur \(X\) qu'elle définit (supposant pour simplifier que \(s(S)\) est fermé), on a alors des isomorphismes canoniques de \(\mathscr{O}_X\)-algèbres augmentées:

\[ \tag{4.4} s^*(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^n)=\mathscr{O}_X/\mathscr{J}^{n+1},\quad s^*(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^{\infty})= \varprojlim_{n} \mathscr{O}_X/\mathscr{J}^{n+1} \]

Ces isomorphismes sont fonctoriels dans un sens évident par changement de base, et (compte tenu de ce fait) redonnent une caractérisation des faisceaux d'algèbres \(\mathscr{P}_{X/S}^n\) sur \(S\). Si par exemple \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) un corps, alors la donnée d'une section \(s\) de \(X\) sur \(S\) équivaut à la donnée d'un point \(x\) de \(X\) rationnel sur \(k\), et les formules précédentes signifient que l'on a un isomorphisme de \(k\)-algèbres

    Lorsque la catégorie-base \(\mathscr{E}\) est réduite à deux objets \(a,b\) et, en plus des flèches identiques, à deux isomorphismes \(f\colon a\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} b\) et \(g\colon b\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} a\) inverse l'un de l'autre (i.e. \(\mathscr{E}\) est un groupoïde connexe rigide avec deux objets), une catégorie clivée normalisée sur \(\mathscr{E}\) est essentiellement la même chose que le système formé par deux catégories \(\mathscr{F}_a\) et \(\mathscr{F}_b\) et un couple de foncteurs adjoints \(G\colon \mathscr{F}_a\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}_b\) et \(F\colon \mathscr{F}_b\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}_a\), qui soient des équivalences de catégories (donc quasi-inverses l'un de l'autre). On prendra pour \(\mathscr{F}_a\) et \(\mathscr{F}_b\) les catégories fibres de \(\mathscr{F}\), pour \(F\) et \(G\) les foncteurs \(f^*\) et \(g^*\), et les deux isomorphismes

    \[ u\colon FG\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr{F}_a}\qquad v\colon GF\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr{F}_b} \]

    sont \(c_{g,f}\) et \(c_{f,g}\). Les deux conditions usuelles de compatibilité entre \(u\) et \(v\) ne sont autres que la condition 4 \(B)\) pour les composés \(fgf\) et \(gfg\). Il est facile de montrer que ces conditions suffisent à impliquer qu'on a bien un pseudo-foncteur \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{Cat}\).

    Un cas intéressant est celui où l'on a

    \[ \mathscr{F}_b=\mathscr{F}_a^\circ,\quad G=F^\circ,\quad v=u^\circ. \]

    On appelle autodualité dans une catégorie \(\mathscr{C}\), la donnée d'un foncteur \(D\colon \mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{C}^\circ\), et d'un isomorphisme \(u\colon DD^\circ\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr{C}}\), tels que \(u\) et l'isomorphisme \(u^\circ\colon D^\circ D\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr{C}^\circ}\) fassent de \((D,D^\circ)\) un couple de foncteurs adjoints, (nécessairement quasi-inverses l'un de l'autre).     \[ D(u(x))=u(D(x))\qquad \text{pour tout $x\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathscr{C})$.} \]

    Catégories au-dessus d'une catégorie discrète \(\mathscr{E}\). On dit que \(\mathscr{E}\) est une catégorie discrète si toute flèche y est une flèche identique, de sorte que \(\mathscr{E}\) est défini à isomorphisme unique près par la connaissance de l'ensemble \(I=\operatorname{Ob}(\mathscr{E})\). La donnée d'une catégorie \(\mathscr{F}\) au-dessus de \(\mathscr{E}\) équivaut donc (à isomorphisme unique près) à la donnée d'une famille de catégories \(\mathscr{F}_i\) (\(i\in I\)), les catégories fibres.     \[ \mathbf{\Gamma}(\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{E})=\varprojlim\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{E}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\underset{i}\prod \mathscr{E}_i. \]
  6. f)

    Supposons que \(\mathscr{E}\) ait exactement deux objets \(S\) et \(T\), et en plus des morphismes identiques, un morphisme \(f\colon T\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). Alors une catégorie \(\mathscr{F}\) au-dessus de \(\mathscr{E}\) est définie, à \(\mathscr{E}\)-isomorphisme unique près, par la donnée de deux catégories \(\mathscr{F}_S\) et \(\mathscr{F}_T\) et d'un bifoncteur \(H(\eta,\xi)\) sur \(\mathscr{F}_T^\circ\times\mathscr{F}_S\), à valeurs dans \(\mathbf{Ens}\). En effet, si \(\mathscr{F}\) est une catégorie au-dessus de \(\mathscr{E}\), on lui associe les deux catégories-fibres \(\mathscr{F}_S\) et \(\mathscr{F}_T\) et le bifoncteur \(H(\eta,\xi)=\operatorname{Hom}_f(\eta,\xi)\). On laisse au lecteur le soin d'expliciter la construction en sens inverse. Pour que la catégorie envisagée soit fibrée (ou préfibrée, cela revient au même) il faut et il suffit que le foncteur \(H\) soit représentable par rapport à l'argument \(\xi\). Pour qu'elle soit co-fibrée, il faut et il suffit que \(H\) soit représentable par rapport à l'argument \(\eta\).

  7. g)

    Soit \(\mathscr{F}=\mathscr{C}\times\mathscr{E}\), considérée comme catégorie au-dessus de \(\mathscr{E}\) grâce à \(\mathrm{pr}_2\). Alors \(\mathscr{F}\) est fibrée et co-fibrée sur \(\mathscr{E}\), et est même munie d'un scindage et d'un co-scindage canonique, correspondant au foncteur constant sur \(\mathscr{E}\), resp. sur \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\), à valeurs dans \(\mathbf{Cat}\), de valeur \(\mathscr{C}\). On a

    \[ \mathbf{\Gamma}(\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{E})\simeq\operatorname{\mathbf{Hom}}(\mathscr{E},\mathscr{C}) \]

Il résulte de 7 dans le cas a) et de 5 dans le cas b), que \(\mathrm{H}^1_{\mathrm{t}}(\overline{U},\overline{F})\) s'identifie au sous-ensemble \(\mathrm{H}^1(\overline{U},\overline{F})\) formé des classes de \(\overline{F}\)-torseurs dont l'image inverse sur \(\widetilde{U}\) est triviale. D'autre part un raisonnement classique (cf. IX 5, p. ) montre que l'ensemble des éléments de \(\mathrm{H}^1(\overline{U},\overline{F})\) dont l'image inverse sur \(\widetilde{U}\) est triviale s'identifie à \(\mathrm{H}^1(\pi_1^{\mathrm{t}}(\overline{U}),\mathrm{H}^0(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{F})).\) On obtient ainsi un isomorphisme canonique
